newsitem.title: UK: Britain challenges IRA to end violence.
newsitem.headline: Britain challenges IRA to end violence.

text.p: Britain challenged the IRA to end its war against London's rule on Sunday after a week of Northern Ireland tumult that culminated in tense but peaceful parades by pro-British Protestants.

"Let the IRA/Sinn Fein make their decision, the ball is in their court," Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam declared as an uneasy calm took hold in the province after sporadic overnight rioting in two cities.

Britain, the United States and Ireland praised the Protestant Orange Order for scrapping four of hundreds of Saturday parades to avoid inflaming Catholic anger on the "Glorious 12th of July," its most cherished anniversary.

But the Irish Republican Army and its political arm, Sinn Fein, came under intense pressure to end a guerrilla war against British rule that has polarised Protestants and Catholics. Moderate Catholic nationalist leader John Hume hailed the "moral courge" of the Orange Order for calling off four controversial marches.
Hume, leader of the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) urged all sides to seize a chance for progress.

"Let us now move forward from the constructive decisions by the Orange Order and build upon that, and let's work to keep building that new atmosphere in order to create an agreed society for the first time," Hume said on BBC television.
British Prime Minister Tony Blair has signalled that Sinn Fein could enter Northern Ireland peace talks six weeks after an unequivocal end to IRA violence.
"Having done that I think that now the IRA should declare a total end to their campaign and create a totally peaceful atmosphere in which the dialogue would take place," Hume said.
But Protestant political leader and IRA scourge David Trimble warned that there was too much "wishful thinking" about the intentions of the IRA and Sinn Fein.
He says Sinn Fein would be left in a wilderness if the guerrillas continued to refuse to surrender arms.
"The reality is that Sinn Fein/IRA are committed to violence in order to achieve objectives that no democrat can support," Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) chief Trimble declared.

"What the Prime Minister and the government are trying to do only makes sense on the basis of leaving Sinn Fein behind, and consequently for the democratic parties to be discussing among themselves," he said.
On the eve of traditional Protestant marches to celebrate Saturday's anniversary, the IRA wounded three soldiers and two police officers in an ambush in north Belfast.
IRA activists were also suspected of a having fired a mortar that exploded harmlessly near a security base in the village of Newtownhamilton close to the border with Ireland.

Protestant politicians said the attacks, and the wounding of two Protestant teenagers by unidentified republican gunmen in north Belfast, were a bid to foment sectarian strife and destabilise the region at one of its most sensitive periods.

Police fired plastic bullets to disperse rioters in Londonderry and Belfast overnight after thousands of Protestants held parades on their most hallowed day, the 307th anniversary of Protestant battlefield victories over the Catholic Irish.
In Londonderry on Saturday Irish nationalist youths attacked police with stones, petrol-bombs and catapults firing ball-bearings, security sources said.
"A large number of commercial premises have been damaged. A number of police were injured but none of them seriously," a spokesman for the Royal Ulster Constabulary police said.
U.S. President Bill Clinton praised the Orange Order for rerouting its parades and condemned as "inexcusable" the attacks on security forces and the two youths.

"I hope that the people of both communities redouble their efforts to reach accommodation on other contentious parades in a spirit of goodwill and generosity and reject the inexcusable violence that we saw in Northern Ireland today," he said.
